content_html:
What Are Macronutrients?

Macronutrients are the nutrients your body needs in large quantities every day. They supply energy and build or repair tissues. All three — protein, fats and carbohydrates — appear on every nutrition label and form the backbone of every meal you cook. Compare them with micronutrients (vitamins and minerals), which are needed in tiny amounts and do not supply energy. Getting the distinction clear is the foundation of this entire unit.

Protein — Functions, Sources and Quality

Protein builds and repairs muscle, makes enzymes and hormones, and supports immune function. The body breaks protein down into amino acids. Of the 20 amino acids in food, nine are essential — we cannot make them ourselves and must eat them. This is where high biological value (HBV) protein comes in. Meat, fish, eggs, dairy, and soya beans all supply HBV protein. In contrast, most plant proteins (beans, lentils, nuts, cereals) are low biological value (LBV) — they’re missing at least one essential amino acid.

Key Fact

HBV proteins (meat, fish, eggs, dairy, soya) contain all nine essential amino acids. LBV proteins (beans, lentils, most cereals) are missing at least one. Vegetarians and vegans can meet all amino acid needs by combining LBV sources.

Protein Complementation

Protein complementation means combining two or more LBV protein sources in the same meal so that the amino acids missing from one are supplied by the other. The classic examples are beans on toast (haricot beans + wheat), rice and peas (rice + kidney beans), and hummus and pitta (chickpeas + wheat). For a vegan teenager eating no animal products, this technique is essential to avoid protein deficiency.

Protein Alternatives

The spec names four main protein alternatives for vegetarian and vegan diets. TVP (textured vegetable protein) is made from defatted soya flour; it absorbs flavour well and can replace mince in a bolognese. Soya is the only plant food that is naturally HBV. Mycoprotein (sold as Quorn) is made from a fungus and is high in fibre as well as protein. Tofu is set soya curd; it has a neutral flavour and takes on marinades readily when diced for a stir-fry.

Students often write that plant proteins are “bad” or “incomplete” and leave it there. This misses the point. LBV proteins are perfectly healthy — they are simply missing one or more essential amino acids on their own. By using complementation (beans on toast, rice and peas, lentil soup with a bread roll), a vegan or vegetarian can get every essential amino acid they need without eating any animal products. Soya is actually HBV and is nutritionally equivalent to meat protein in that respect.

Deficiency and Excess

Protein deficiency is rare in the UK but causes kwashiorkor in severe cases (muscle wasting, swollen abdomen, poor immunity). Mild deficiency leads to slow growth in children and poor wound healing. Excess protein is not stored — the nitrogen is excreted as urea, putting extra strain on the kidneys. Most UK adults consume more protein than the Reference Nutrient Intake (RNI) of around 0.75 g per kg body weight per day.

Fats — Types, Functions and Effects

Fats supply more than twice the energy of protein or carbohydrate per gram (9 kcal/g versus 4 kcal/g). They insulate the body, protect organs, carry fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K, and are essential for hormone production. There are two main types.

Saturated fats are solid at room temperature. Think butter, lard, the white fat on a lamb chop, the cream in a dessert. High intake raises LDL (“bad”) cholesterol, which is a risk factor for coronary heart disease (CHD). Current guidelines recommend that saturated fats make up no more than 11% of daily energy intake.

Unsaturated fats are liquid at room temperature and come in two sub-types: monounsaturated (olive oil, avocado, rapeseed oil) and polyunsaturated (sunflower oil, oily fish, walnuts). Replacing saturated fats with unsaturated fats can reduce LDL cholesterol. Oily fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines) are particularly rich in omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids, which support heart health.

A common exam error is to write “fat is bad” and then list butter as the only source. Remember: unsaturated fats are essential. Without them, you cannot absorb vitamins A, D, E and K, and you risk deficiency of those nutrients too. The exam expects you to distinguish between saturated and unsaturated, name sources of each, and link saturated fat excess to CHD via raised LDL cholesterol. Fat deficiency — though rare — causes poor absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, dry skin, hormonal disruption and lack of energy.

Carbohydrates — Structure, Functions and Fibre

Carbohydrates are the body’s preferred energy source, supplying 4 kcal per gram. They come in three structural forms:

  • Monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose) — the simplest sugars; absorbed directly into the blood.
  • Disaccharides (sucrose = glucose + fructose; lactose = glucose + galactose; maltose = glucose + glucose) — two monosaccharides joined together.
  • Polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, dietary fibre (NSP)) — long chains of monosaccharides.

Starch is found in bread, pasta, rice, potatoes, cereals and oats. It is the slow-release fuel that should form the majority of a GCSE student’s energy intake. Free sugars (those added to food or naturally present in honey, syrups and fruit juices) should make up no more than 5% of total energy intake. Dietary fibre keeps the gut healthy, prevents constipation and reduces the risk of bowel cancer and type 2 diabetes.

Key Fact

Carbohydrates: monosaccharides (glucose), disaccharides (sucrose), polysaccharides (starch, dietary fibre). Excess free sugars cause tooth decay and contribute to obesity and type 2 diabetes. The recommended maximum for free sugars is 5% of total energy intake.

Deficiency of carbohydrates means the body switches to fat then protein for fuel, producing ketone bodies, which can cause fatigue, brain fog and, in extreme cases, a dangerous condition called ketoacidosis. Deficiency of dietary fibre causes constipation and increases the long-term risk of bowel cancer. Excess carbohydrate (especially refined sugars) is stored as body fat once glycogen stores are full, contributing to obesity.

Micronutrients — The Small but Essential Nutrients

Micronutrients are vitamins and minerals needed in tiny quantities — milligrams or micrograms rather than grams. Unlike macronutrients, they do not supply energy; instead they regulate countless body processes, from bone formation to immune defence to energy release from food. Missing even one regularly causes a specific deficiency disease. The exam expects you to know each one’s functions, main sources, and effects of deficiency and excess.

Fat-Soluble Vitamins

Fat-soluble vitamins are stored in the liver and body fat, so they do not need to be eaten every day — but they can build up to toxic levels if consumed in very high doses (excess). There are four: A, D, E and K.

  • Vitamin A — needed for vision in dim light (rhodopsin production), healthy skin, and immune function. Sources: liver, oily fish, dairy, eggs; also from beta-carotene in orange and yellow vegetables (carrots, sweet potato, butternut squash). Deficiency causes night blindness and dry skin.
  • Vitamin D — essential for absorbing calcium and phosphorus, so it underpins strong bones and teeth. The body makes it when skin is exposed to sunlight; dietary sources include oily fish, eggs, fortified cereals and fortified spreads. Deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults (soft, painful bones).
  • Vitamin E — an antioxidant that protects cell membranes from oxidative damage. Sources include vegetable oils, nuts, seeds and avocado. Deficiency is rare in healthy adults but can cause nerve damage.
  • Vitamin K — essential for blood clotting and bone health. Main sources: green leafy vegetables (kale, spinach, broccoli), vegetable oils, fermented foods. Deficiency causes impaired blood clotting.
Key Fact

Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K are stored in the liver and body fat. Excess can be toxic. Deficiency of vitamin D causes rickets in children; deficiency of vitamin A causes night blindness.

Water-Soluble Vitamins — The B Group and Vitamin C

Water-soluble vitamins dissolve in water and cannot be stored in large amounts, so they need to be eaten regularly. They are also easily lost during food preparation and cooking — a critical exam point.

  • B1 (thiamin) — needed for energy release from carbohydrates. Sources: pork, fortified cereals, nuts, peas. Deficiency causes beriberi (nerve damage, muscle weakness).
  • B2 (riboflavin) — supports energy metabolism and healthy skin. Sources: milk, eggs, liver, fortified cereals.
  • B3 (niacin) — needed for energy metabolism and DNA repair. Sources: meat, fish, peanuts, fortified flour. Severe deficiency causes pellagra.
  • Folic acid (folate) — essential for making new red blood cells and for healthy fetal development (prevents neural tube defects). Sources: green leafy vegetables, beans, fortified bread. Deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia; pregnant women are advised to supplement.
  • B12 (cobalamin) — required for red blood cell formation and maintaining the nervous system. Sources: meat, fish, dairy, eggs (virtually absent from non-fortified plant foods). Deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia and nerve damage; vegans must supplement or eat fortified foods.
  • Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) — needed for collagen synthesis (skin, blood vessels, wound healing), immune function, and iron absorption from plant foods. Sources: fresh fruit (oranges, kiwi, strawberries), peppers, broccoli, potatoes. Deficiency causes scurvy (bleeding gums, slow wound healing).

Vitamins C and the B-group are water-soluble and heat-sensitive, so they leach into cooking water and are destroyed by prolonged heat. When you boil broccoli, the vitamin C and folate dissolve into the water — which is then poured down the drain. To minimise losses: use the minimum water possible; steam rather than boil (the food doesn’t sit in water); use short cooking times; prepare vegetables just before cooking (chopping increases surface area and speeds up oxidation); avoid keeping cooked vegetables warm for long periods. These facts are frequently tested with a “describe” command word.

Key Minerals

The spec lists six minerals you must know: calcium, iron, sodium, fluoride, iodine and phosphorus.

  • Calcium — builds and maintains bones and teeth, assists muscle contraction and nerve function. Sources: milk, cheese, yoghurt, fortified plant milks, canned fish with bones (sardines), dark green vegetables. Deficiency causes rickets (children) or osteoporosis (adults).
  • Iron — needed for making haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in red blood cells. Sources: red meat (haem iron, absorbed most efficiently), liver, fortified cereals, lentils, dark green vegetables. Deficiency causes iron-deficiency anaemia (fatigue, pale skin, breathlessness). Vitamin C consumed at the same meal increases non-haem iron absorption from plant foods.
  • Sodium (salt) — regulates fluid balance and nerve impulses. Too much raises blood pressure (hypertension), increasing the risk of stroke and CHD. Most dietary sodium comes from processed foods. The Reference Intake for adults is 2.4 g sodium (6 g salt) per day.
  • Fluoride — strengthens tooth enamel and reduces tooth decay. Sources: fluoridated water, tea, fish. Excess causes dental fluorosis (mottled teeth).
  • Iodine — essential for making thyroid hormones, which regulate metabolism. Sources: milk, dairy, seafood, some fortified foods. Deficiency causes goitre (enlarged thyroid gland) and, in pregnancy, can impair the baby’s brain development.
  • Phosphorus — works alongside calcium to build bones and teeth; also involved in energy metabolism. Sources: meat, fish, dairy, eggs, cereals.
Key Fact

Iron makes haemoglobin to carry oxygen in blood. Deficiency causes iron-deficiency anaemia. Calcium builds bones and teeth; deficiency causes rickets (children) or osteoporosis (adults). Vitamin C increases absorption of non-haem iron from plant sources.

Antioxidants — Protecting Cells from Damage

Antioxidants neutralise free radicals — unstable molecules that damage cell membranes and DNA. The three antioxidant vitamins on the spec are:

  • Vitamin A (from beta-carotene in plant foods) — protects cells in the respiratory and digestive tracts.
  • Vitamin C — water-soluble antioxidant; active in the fluid inside cells and in blood plasma.
  • Vitamin E — fat-soluble antioxidant; embedded in cell membranes where it prevents oxidative damage to fats.

Eating a diet rich in colourful fruits and vegetables — a Greek salad of tomatoes, peppers, cucumber and olive oil, or a fruit salad of kiwi, strawberries and orange — provides a wide range of antioxidants. This is part of the evidence base behind the government’s five-a-day guidance.

Many students incorrectly state that all vitamins are lost when you boil vegetables. Only water-soluble vitamins (B-group and C) leach into cooking water. Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K) do not dissolve in water and are not lost by boiling — though they can be damaged by prolonged very high heat. The practical implication is: to preserve vitamin C in a stir-fry, use high heat for a short time with very little water; to preserve vitamin C in boiled broccoli, steam instead and serve immediately.

Water and Hydration

Water is not classified as a macronutrient or micronutrient but is essential for life. Its key functions are: transporting nutrients and oxygen in the blood; removing waste products as urine; regulating body temperature through sweating; acting as a lubricant in joints; and supporting digestion. The body loses water through breathing, sweating, urinating and in faeces. Adults should drink approximately 6–8 cups (around 1.5–2 litres) of fluid per day. More is needed in hot weather, during exercise, and when ill. Dehydration causes headaches, fatigue, reduced concentration and, in severe cases, organ failure.

lesson_title: Nutritional Needs, Life Stages and Diet Planning
content_html:
Guidelines for a Healthy Diet — The Eatwell Guide

The Eatwell Guide is the UK government’s model for a balanced diet. It divides food into five groups and shows roughly what proportion of your plate each should occupy. Because the exam focuses on applying the guide to real meals rather than simply listing percentages, it is worth understanding what each segment means in practice.

  • Fruit and vegetables (roughly one third of the plate) — include fresh, frozen, dried, canned and juiced varieties. At least five 80 g portions per day is the guidance. They supply vitamins, minerals, fibre and antioxidants.
  • Starchy carbohydrates (roughly one third) — bread, pasta, rice, potatoes, oats. Choose wholegrain versions where possible for more fibre and B vitamins.
  • Dairy and dairy alternatives — milk, cheese, yoghurt, and fortified plant milks. Main sources of calcium and iodine.
  • Protein foods — beans, pulses, fish, eggs, meat and meat alternatives (TVP, tofu, mycoprotein). Eat at least two portions of fish per week, one of which should be oily.
  • Oils and spreads — use in small amounts and choose unsaturated options (olive oil, rapeseed oil) rather than butter or lard.

Foods high in fat, salt and sugar — biscuits, cakes, crisps, fizzy drinks — are shown outside the main segments. They are not necessary for a healthy diet and should be eaten less frequently and in small amounts.

Key Fact

The Eatwell Guide has five food groups. Fruit and vegetables and starchy carbohydrates each form roughly one third of the daily plate. Protein foods, dairy and dairy alternatives make up most of the rest. Oils and spreads are used in small amounts. Foods high in fat, salt and sugar sit outside the guide.

Portion Size and Costing

When planning a meal, portion size matters for both nutrition and cost. A portion of meat or fish is typically 80–100 g; a portion of cooked pasta or rice is around 180 g. Planning meals in advance, writing a shopping list, using seasonal ingredients, buying own-brand products, and avoiding food waste all reduce the cost of a balanced diet. Costing a recipe means calculating the ingredient cost per serving: divide the cost of the whole pack by the number of portions the pack makes, then add up all the ingredient costs for one serving.

How Nutritional Needs Change Across Life Stages

The body’s needs are not fixed throughout life. Growth, hormone changes, activity levels and the gradual slowing of metabolism all shift what nutrients we need most. The exam lists four life stages to know in detail.

Young Children (1–5 years)

Young children are growing rapidly and need relatively high energy, protein, calcium and vitamin D for bone development. However, their stomachs are small, so meals should be nutritionally dense rather than bulky. Whole (full-fat) milk rather than skimmed milk is recommended up to age 2 because growing toddlers need the fat and fat-soluble vitamins. Salt intake should be kept very low (less than 2 g/day for children aged 1–3). Young children are at higher risk of iron deficiency because they are growing fast; iron-rich foods (red meat, fortified cereals, beans) should be included regularly.

Teenagers

Adolescence brings the biggest growth spurt since infancy. Teenagers have high energy needs, especially if active, and need more protein for muscle development. Calcium and vitamin D are critical: bone density peaks in your early twenties, so what you eat during your teenage years directly affects your risk of osteoporosis decades later. Teenage girls who have started their periods have significantly higher iron needs than boys (because of menstrual blood loss) — and iron-deficiency anaemia is one of the most common nutritional deficiencies in adolescent girls. Folate is also important for all teenagers for healthy cell division.

Adults

Adults have lower energy needs relative to body size than teenagers. The focus shifts to maintaining a healthy body weight, keeping cardiovascular risk low (limiting saturated fat and salt), and eating adequate fibre to reduce the risk of bowel disease and type 2 diabetes. Pregnant and breastfeeding women have additional requirements: folic acid in the first trimester reduces the risk of neural tube defects; iron supports the growing foetus and replaces maternal losses; calcium and vitamin D support fetal bone development; and energy needs increase in the third trimester and during breastfeeding.

The Elderly

Older adults have lower total energy needs because metabolism slows, but their need for protein, calcium, vitamin D and B12 remains high or even increases. Many elderly people have reduced appetite and may be less active, making every mouthful count nutritionally. Vitamin D synthesis in the skin declines with age, and many older adults spend less time outdoors; supplementation is widely recommended. Risk of osteoporosis increases, making calcium intake critical. Dehydration is common in the elderly because the sense of thirst becomes less reliable with age.

Key Fact

Teenage girls need more iron (to replace menstrual losses) and calcium (for peak bone density). Elderly adults need vitamin D (skin synthesis declines), calcium (osteoporosis risk) and vitamin B12 (absorption declines with age) despite lower overall energy needs.

Planning for Specific Dietary Groups

The exam expects you to plan a balanced meal for four specific dietary groups. Each one requires thought about nutrient gaps and practical substitutions.

A vegetarian diet excludes meat and fish. A vegan diet excludes all animal products. Both must plan carefully to avoid deficiencies. Key nutrients at risk in vegan diets: vitamin B12 (only in animal foods or fortified products), vitamin D (few dietary plant sources), calcium (dairy is the main UK source — must use fortified plant milks or eat plenty of kale and tofu), iron (non-haem iron from plant foods is less well absorbed — eat with vitamin C), omega-3 fats (oily fish is absent — flaxseed, walnuts, algae-based supplements). Protein: use complementation and soya/tofu/mycoprotein.

Coeliac disease requires a strict gluten-free diet. Gluten is found in wheat, barley and rye — so ordinary bread, pasta, biscuits and cakes are off-limits. Substitutes include rice, maize (corn), potatoes, gluten-free oats, and purpose-made gluten-free products. Cross-contamination in the kitchen must be prevented. Lactose intolerance means the person cannot digest lactose, the sugar in cow’s milk, due to insufficient lactase enzyme. Symptoms include bloating and diarrhoea. Alternatives: lactose-free milk, hard cheeses (lower in lactose), small amounts of yoghurt (fermentation reduces lactose), and calcium-fortified plant milks. A high-fibre diet benefits people at risk of constipation, bowel disease or type 2 diabetes. It should include wholegrain bread and cereals, plenty of vegetables and pulses, and fruit.

Maintaining a Healthy Body Weight

A healthy body weight is maintained when energy intake equals energy expenditure — this is called energy balance. Regular physical activity, eating plenty of fibre (which promotes satiety), limiting high-fat and high-sugar foods, and eating regular meals (which prevents extreme hunger leading to overeating) all support a healthy weight throughout life. Making informed food choices means reading labels, understanding portion sizes, and choosing cooking methods that add less fat (grilling rather than frying, baking rather than deep-frying).

Where Does Energy Come From — and How Much Do You Need?

Every time you move, breathe, digest food or maintain your body temperature, you use energy. That energy comes from the macronutrients in food: carbohydrates and protein each supply 4 kcal (kilocalories) per gram; fat supplies 9 kcal per gram; alcohol supplies 7 kcal per gram (not on the spec but worth knowing for context). The total energy a person needs each day depends on two factors: their basal metabolic rate (BMR) and their physical activity level.

Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR)

BMR is the energy your body burns at rest — doing nothing but keeping the heart beating, the lungs breathing and the cells functioning. It accounts for roughly 60–75% of total daily energy use. Several factors affect BMR:

  • Age — BMR declines with age as muscle mass decreases and metabolism slows. A 16-year-old has a higher BMR per kilogram of body weight than a 60-year-old.
  • Gender — males typically have higher BMR than females of the same weight because they generally have more muscle mass. Muscle tissue burns more energy at rest than fat tissue.
  • Body composition — a person with more lean muscle mass has a higher BMR. A marathon runner has a higher BMR than a sedentary person of the same weight.
  • Hormones — thyroid hormones regulate metabolic rate; an overactive thyroid raises BMR, an underactive thyroid lowers it.
  • Pregnancy — BMR increases during pregnancy because the body is supporting fetal development and preparing for breastfeeding.
Key Fact

BMR is the energy the body needs at complete rest to maintain vital functions. It is affected by age (declines with age), gender (males typically higher), body composition (more muscle = higher BMR), hormones and life stage (pregnancy increases it). BMR accounts for approximately 60–75% of total daily energy expenditure.

Physical Activity Level (PAL)

Physical activity level (PAL) is a multiplier that reflects how much energy a person uses through movement on top of their BMR. A sedentary adult (desk job, little exercise) has a PAL of roughly 1.4; a moderately active adult (some walking, 3–4 sessions of exercise per week) has a PAL of around 1.6–1.7; a very active person (manual job or elite athlete in daily training) can have a PAL above 1.9.

Total daily energy requirement = BMR × PAL. For example, a 15-year-old girl with a BMR of 1,400 kcal/day who plays netball four times a week and walks to school (PAL ≈ 1.7) needs approximately 2,380 kcal per day. If she eats less than this consistently, she loses weight; if she eats more, she gains weight.

Energy Balance

Energy balance means intake equals expenditure. Positive energy balance (more in than out) leads to weight gain over time, as excess energy is stored as body fat. Negative energy balance (more out than in) leads to weight loss. For a person trying to manage their weight, increasing PAL (more physical activity) or reducing energy-dense food intake are both effective strategies.

A common misconception is that eating fat directly causes weight gain while eating carbohydrate does not. In reality, weight gain comes from positive energy balance — consuming more total kilocalories than you expend. Fat contributes more kcal per gram (9 kcal/g vs 4 kcal/g for carbohydrate or protein), so high-fat foods are energy-dense and easy to overconsume. But a diet high in refined carbohydrates and sugar can equally lead to positive energy balance and weight gain. The focus should be on total energy intake relative to PAL, not on demonising any single macronutrient.

Recommended Percentages of Energy from Nutrients

Current guidelines specify that the balance of macronutrients in the diet should be:

  • Protein: 15% of total energy intake.
  • Fat: 35% or less of total energy intake (of which no more than 11% from saturated fats).
  • Carbohydrate: 50% of total energy intake — of which 45% from starches, lactose in milk and fruit sugars, and a maximum of 5% from free sugars (added sugars, honey, syrups and fruit juices).

These are percentage targets for the whole diet over time, not for every individual meal. In practice, a typical UK diet has too many free sugars and saturated fats and not enough dietary fibre. A dinner of grilled salmon (protein and unsaturated fat), a large portion of brown rice (complex carbohydrate) and steamed broccoli (fibre and micronutrients) moves the balance in the right direction.

Key Fact

Target energy split: protein 15%, fat 35% or less, carbohydrate 50% (of which maximum 5% from free sugars, 45% from starches, lactose and fruit sugars). These are the exact figures the written paper may ask for directly.

Carrying Out Nutritional Analysis

Nutritional analysis means calculating how much energy and how many nutrients a recipe or meal provides per serving. In a school kitchen or professional setting this is done using nutritional analysis software (e.g. Nutritionix, Cronometer or bespoke food-technology software). In an exam, it is done using food tables (printed tables of nutritional values per 100 g for each ingredient).

The method is: identify each ingredient and its weight in the recipe; look up its nutritional values per 100 g in the food table; scale to the actual weight used (e.g. if the table gives values per 100 g and you use 250 g, multiply by 2.5); add up all the ingredient contributions to get the total for the whole recipe; then divide by the number of portions to get the value per serving. This can be done for energy (kcal), protein (g), fat (g), carbohydrate (g), fibre (g), and individual vitamins or minerals.

Once you have the analysis, you can compare it to the Dietary Reference Values (DRVs) or Reference Intakes (RIs) for the target person and identify nutrients that are too high or too low. If the recipe is too high in saturated fat, you might substitute full-fat cream for a lower-fat yoghurt, or grill the meat instead of frying. If it is low in iron, you could add spinach, kidney beans or fortified cereal to the recipe.

The written paper may present a recipe analysis and ask you to suggest modifications. The key is to apply the energy percentages and RIs as benchmarks. Common modifications: (1) Too much saturated fat — swap butter for an unsaturated spread or olive oil; use skimmed or semi-skimmed milk instead of full-fat; remove the skin from chicken before cooking. (2) Too much salt — use herbs and spices to season instead of added salt; choose low-salt stock cubes; reduce the amount of processed ingredients. (3) Too little fibre — swap white pasta for wholemeal; add lentils or beans; include more vegetables. (4) Too much free sugar — reduce the amount of added sugar; use fresh fruit to sweeten instead of syrup or jam. Each modification should be linked back to a specific health benefit.

lesson_title: Diet, Nutrition and Health — Diet-Related Disease
content_html:
The Link Between Diet and Health

What you eat does not only affect your weight — it shapes your long-term risk of several serious conditions. The written paper expects you to explain these relationships as cause-and-effect chains, not just lists. For every condition below, you need to know: which dietary factors increase the risk, what happens in the body as a result, and what dietary changes reduce the risk. Starting with a clear chain — “high saturated fat intake raises LDL cholesterol, which builds up in artery walls, narrowing them, which raises the risk of heart attack” — is far more valuable than a list of “foods to avoid”.

Obesity

Obesity results from sustained positive energy balance — eating more calories than the body uses — so the excess energy is stored as body fat. Dietary risk factors include: a diet high in energy-dense foods (those rich in fat and/or free sugars); large portion sizes; frequent consumption of processed snack foods, fast food and sugary drinks; and low intake of fibre (which promotes satiety). Obesity raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, coronary heart disease, certain cancers, osteoarthritis and mental health difficulties. Dietary modifications to prevent or reduce obesity: reduce energy-dense foods; increase fibre (promotes fullness); increase fruit and vegetables; choose leaner cooking methods (grill or steam rather than deep-fry); reduce alcohol (which is energy-dense but nutrient-poor); control portion sizes.

Cardiovascular Health — CHD and High Blood Pressure

Coronary heart disease (CHD) develops when the coronary arteries supplying the heart become narrowed or blocked. The key dietary chain is: a high intake of saturated fats raises the level of LDL (“bad”) cholesterol in the blood. Over time, LDL cholesterol deposits form plaques on the artery walls (a process called atherosclerosis), narrowing the arteries. A narrowed coronary artery reduces blood flow to the heart, which can cause angina (chest pain) or, if a clot blocks the artery completely, a heart attack.

Hypertension (high blood pressure) is independently linked to a high sodium (salt) intake. Excess salt causes the body to retain water, increasing blood volume and pressure against artery walls. High blood pressure damages artery walls, speeding up atherosclerosis and raising the risk of stroke and heart failure. The maximum recommended adult intake is 6 g of salt (2.4 g sodium) per day; most UK adults exceed this because processed foods, bread and ready meals are the main contributors.

Key Fact

High saturated fat → raises LDL cholesterol → atherosclerosis (plaque build-up in artery walls) → narrowed coronary arteries → reduced blood flow to the heart → angina or heart attack. High salt intake → raised blood pressure (hypertension) → increased risk of stroke and CHD.

Many students write only that a “bad diet causes obesity and then disease”, and stop there. This misses several independent dietary links. A person of healthy weight can still develop CHD from a diet high in saturated fat (because LDL cholesterol rises regardless of BMI). A slim person can develop iron-deficiency anaemia if they avoid red meat, fortified cereals and vitamin-C-rich foods. A child of any weight can develop rickets if their diet is low in vitamin D and calcium. The exam rewards students who can explain each disease through its own specific dietary mechanism, not just through obesity as an intermediate step.

Bone Health — Rickets and Osteoporosis

Bones need calcium and vitamin D to develop and stay strong. Without adequate calcium, the body draws calcium from bones to maintain blood levels, gradually weakening them. Without vitamin D, calcium cannot be absorbed from the gut, so even a calcium-rich diet does not fully protect bones if vitamin D is deficient.

  • Rickets (in children) — caused by deficiency of vitamin D and/or calcium. The leg bones soften and bow outwards because they cannot mineralise properly. Dietary sources of vitamin D include oily fish, eggs and fortified foods; sunlight exposure also triggers skin synthesis. Risk groups: children in the UK who have limited sun exposure, especially in winter.
  • Osteoporosis (in adults) — gradual loss of bone density, making bones fragile and prone to fracture. Risk factors include a long-term low-calcium diet, vitamin D deficiency, low oestrogen (after the menopause in women), smoking and physical inactivity. Peak bone mass is reached in the early twenties, so calcium and vitamin D intake during childhood and adolescence directly affects long-term osteoporosis risk.

Dental Health

Tooth decay (dental caries) occurs when bacteria in the mouth ferment sugars to produce acids, which dissolve tooth enamel. Frequent consumption of free sugars — particularly between meals, when saliva flow is lower — increases the time teeth are exposed to acid attack. Sugary drinks, sweets, biscuits, cakes and fruit juices are the main culprits. Fluoride strengthens tooth enamel and increases its resistance to acid, which is why fluoridated water and fluoride toothpaste are public health measures. Calcium and phosphorus in dairy products help remineralise enamel. Reducing the frequency and amount of free sugar consumed is the most effective dietary strategy to protect dental health.

Iron-Deficiency Anaemia

Iron-deficiency anaemia develops when the body does not have enough iron to make adequate haemoglobin. Haemoglobin is the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen to every tissue; when levels are low, the body cannot supply enough oxygen, causing tiredness, pale skin, breathlessness and poor concentration. Risk groups: teenage girls and adult women (menstrual losses); pregnant women (iron demand rises to support the fetus and placenta); young children (rapid growth increases demand); and people following vegetarian or vegan diets (plant sources of iron are less well absorbed). Dietary strategies: eat iron-rich foods (red meat, liver, oily fish, fortified cereals, lentils, dark green vegetables); eat these alongside vitamin C (orange juice, pepper, tomato) to enhance non-haem iron absorption; avoid drinking tea with meals (tannins in tea inhibit iron absorption).

Key Fact

Iron-deficiency anaemia risk groups: teenage girls, adult women, pregnant women, young children, vegetarians and vegans. Eating iron-rich foods alongside vitamin C increases absorption of non-haem iron from plant sources. Tea at mealtimes reduces iron absorption.

Type 2 Diabetes

Type 2 diabetes occurs when the body becomes resistant to insulin or cannot produce enough insulin to keep blood glucose at a normal level. After eating, blood glucose rises; insulin is released by the pancreas to move glucose into cells for energy. In type 2 diabetes, cells become less responsive to insulin (insulin resistance), and blood glucose remains elevated. Over time, high blood glucose damages blood vessels and nerves, increasing the risk of heart disease, kidney failure, blindness and amputations.

The main dietary risk factors for type 2 diabetes are: obesity (excess body fat, especially around the abdomen, is strongly associated with insulin resistance); a high intake of refined carbohydrates and free sugars (which cause rapid spikes in blood glucose, repeatedly demanding high insulin output); and low dietary fibre intake (fibre slows glucose absorption, reducing blood glucose spikes). Dietary management after diagnosis: reduce free sugars and refined carbohydrates; choose low-glycaemic-index foods (wholegrain bread, oats, lentils, pulses); increase dietary fibre; control portion sizes; lose weight if overweight to improve insulin sensitivity.

These are the chains the exam tests most often:

  • CHD: high saturated fat → raised LDL cholesterol → atherosclerosis → narrowed arteries → heart attack.
  • Hypertension: high salt intake → fluid retention → raised blood pressure → stroke/CHD.
  • Type 2 diabetes: excess free sugars and refined carbs + obesity → insulin resistance → chronic raised blood glucose → damage to blood vessels and nerves.
  • Anaemia: low iron intake (or poor absorption) → insufficient haemoglobin → reduced oxygen delivery → fatigue and pale skin.
  • Dental decay: frequent free sugar intake → bacterial fermentation → acid attack on enamel → tooth decay.
  • Rickets/osteoporosis: low vitamin D and/or calcium → poor bone mineralisation → soft bones (children) or fragile bones (adults).

lesson_title: Why Food is Cooked and Heat Transfer
content_html:
Why Do We Cook Food?

Most food can be eaten raw, but cooking transforms it in ways that make it safer, tastier and more nutritious. There are five core reasons why we cook food, and the written paper expects you to know all of them.

First, cooking makes food safe to eat. Raw chicken can harbour dangerous bacteria. When a chicken breast reaches a core temperature of 75°C, the heat kills pathogenic microorganisms and the meat becomes safe. Second, cooking develops flavours. A raw onion is sharp and pungent; fry it slowly and the sugars caramelise, creating a sweet, golden depth that no raw onion can match. Third, cooking improves texture. Raw potato is starchy and hard; boiling it gelatinises the starch and softens the cell walls, giving it the floury texture we expect. Fourth, cooking improves shelf life. Blanching vegetables before freezing destroys the enzymes that cause spoilage, extending how long the food stays usable. Fifth, cooking gives variety in the diet — the same chicken breast can be poached, roasted, grilled or stir-fried, each method producing a different colour, flavour and texture.

Key Fact

The five reasons food is cooked: make food safe; develop flavours; improve texture; improve shelf life; give variety in the diet. All five are expected in the written paper.

How Heat Is Transferred to Food

Heat does not simply “jump” into food — it travels by one of three distinct mechanisms: conduction, convection, and radiation. Understanding which mechanism is at work in a given cooking method is a high-tariff skill.

Conduction

Conduction happens when heat passes through direct contact, molecule to molecule. Place a frying pan on a hob. The burner heats the metal base of the pan; the molecules at the bottom vibrate faster and pass their energy along to neighbouring molecules. The heat travels upward through the pan until the cooking surface is hot enough to fry. When you lay a chicken breast into the hot pan, conduction transfers heat from the pan surface into the meat. Metals are good conductors — this is why a metal frying pan heats quickly. Food itself is a poor conductor, which is why the centre of a thick piece of meat takes much longer to cook than the outside.

Convection

Convection relies on the movement of a fluid — either liquid or gas. When you heat a pan of water, the water at the bottom nearest the heat source warms first, becomes less dense, and rises. Cooler water from the top falls to replace it, setting up a circulation known as a convection current. This is why a sauce heats unevenly if you leave it still — only the bottom is directly heated by conduction, and without stirring, the top stays cool. Agitation — stirring with a wooden spoon or whisk — forces the hot liquid to mix evenly with the cooler liquid, distributing the heat throughout the sauce. In an oven, hot air rises and circulates in the same way; a fan-assisted oven speeds this up by moving the air artificially.

When you make a béchamel sauce, conduction heats the milk and roux from below, while convection currents try to circulate the liquid. However, starch granules can settle at the bottom and scorch before the top of the sauce even heats through. Stirring constantly does two things: it breaks up the convection pattern so all the sauce heats evenly, and it keeps the starch granules suspended so they don’t stick and burn. Without agitation, the starch at the bottom scorches while the top stays raw — you end up with a lumpy, bitter sauce. This is why the spec specifically lists “the need for agitation” when cooking a sauce.

Radiation

Radiation transfers heat as infrared waves, which do not need any medium — they travel through air just as sunlight travels through space. The grill in an oven is the clearest classroom example. When you place halloumi or tomatoes under a grill, the glowing element emits infrared radiation that travels downward, striking the surface of the food and heating it directly. No air needs to move; no contact is required. This is why the top surface of grilled bread toasts and browns rapidly while the underside stays pale until turned over. Radiation browns and chars surfaces in a way that conduction and convection alone cannot.

Key Fact

Conduction: heat passes through direct contact (frying pan to food). Convection: heat moves through circulating currents in liquid or gas (boiling water, oven air). Radiation: heat travels as infrared waves (grill browning a surface).

Selecting the Right Cooking Method

Choosing a cooking method is not just about taste — it also affects the nutritional value and palatability of the finished dish. The spec groups cooking methods into three families:

Water-based methods include steaming, boiling, simmering, blanching, poaching and braising. These use water or steam as the heat-transfer medium. Boiling and simmering use convection currents to heat food evenly throughout. Steaming keeps food above boiling water, so heat reaches it by convection in the steam. Because the food is not submerged, fewer water-soluble vitamins (vitamin C and the B vitamins) leach out — steaming is therefore generally better than boiling for preserving water-soluble vitamins.

Dry methods include baking, roasting, grilling and dry frying. These use hot air (convection) or direct heat (radiation or conduction) without added water or fat. Grilling uses radiation from above; baking and roasting rely on convection in hot oven air. Because no water is present, browning reactions such as dextrinisation (bread crust) and caramelisation (roasted carrots) occur more readily, improving colour and flavour.

Fat-based methods include shallow frying and stir-frying. A small amount of oil is used in the pan; conduction transfers heat from the hot pan surface through the oil to the food. Stir-frying uses very high heat and constant movement over a short time, which preserves texture and much of the vitamin C content of vegetables because the cooking time is brief.

This is a very common misconception. Nutrient loss depends on three factors: temperature, cooking time and whether the food is submerged in water. Water-soluble vitamins (C and B group) leach into cooking water — this is why boiling a broccoli floret for ten minutes destroys most of its vitamin C. Steaming, microwaving or stir-frying the same broccoli for two to three minutes retains far more. Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K) are not lost into water but can be destroyed by very high temperatures over long cooking times. The nutritional impact of a cooking method depends on which vitamins the food contains and how the method treats water-soluble versus fat-soluble nutrients differently.

Marinades and Palatability

Cooking also affects the palatability of food — its overall pleasantness in terms of appearance, colour, flavour, texture, smell and mouthfeel. One specific technique in this area is the use of marinades. When a chicken thigh sits overnight in a yoghurt and lemon juice marinade, the acid in the lemon juice begins to denature the protein in the surface layer of the meat. The protein chains unravel, the texture softens, and the flavours from the marinade penetrate more deeply. When the chicken is then cooked, the denatured protein coagulates and sets in a more flavourful, more tender state than an unmarinated piece would. Acids in marinades (lemon juice, vinegar, wine) are not just for flavour — they are doing chemical work on the protein structure before the heat even begins.

Functional Properties of Proteins

Proteins are not just a nutrient — they are functional ingredients that change their structure when heat, acid or mechanical force is applied. The spec identifies four functional properties of proteins: denaturation, coagulation, gluten formation and foam formation. These four processes underpin almost every baked or cooked protein-rich product, from a Victoria sponge to a quiche Lorraine.

Denaturation

Protein molecules exist in a precise three-dimensional coiled shape, held together by weak chemical bonds. When those bonds are disrupted — by heat, acid, salt or physical beating — the protein unfolds. This is denaturation. Think of the moment a raw egg hits a hot pan: the transparent, runny protein rapidly turns white and opaque as the albumin proteins in the white denature. The process is permanent — you cannot unfry an egg. Acids denature protein too. A lemon juice and olive oil marinade applied to raw salmon begins to denature the surface proteins before any heat is applied. The flesh turns from translucent to opaque, and the texture firms slightly. This is why “ceviche” — raw fish marinated in citrus juice — appears cooked even though no heat has been used.

Coagulation

Once proteins have denatured, continued heating causes them to coagulate: the unfolded chains bond to each other and form a solid, set network. When you bake a quiche, the egg-and-milk custard filling is liquid when it goes into the oven. As the temperature rises above about 70°C, the egg proteins denature and then coagulate, turning the filling from liquid to a solid, sliceable set. Too much heat (or too long in the oven) causes over-coagulation: the protein network contracts, squeezing out water and giving you a rubbery, watery quiche instead of a smooth, creamy one. Temperature control is everything.

Students frequently use these terms interchangeably, but they are two distinct stages. Denaturation is the unfolding of the protein’s shape — the bonds holding the coiled structure are broken and the protein becomes a loose chain. At this point the protein is still a separate molecule. Coagulation only happens afterwards: the loose, denatured chains start bonding to each other, forming a new cross-linked solid structure. So denaturation must happen first; coagulation is what follows. Think of it as “unravel, then re-join”. A 4-mark Explain question may specifically ask you to sequence these two stages — if you confuse them or call them the same process, you will lose marks.

Gluten Formation

Wheat flour contains two proteins: glutenin and gliadin. Individually, these proteins are relatively inert. But add water and work the mixture — kneading bread dough, rubbing fat into flour for pastry, mixing a cake batter — and these proteins combine to form gluten, an elastic network of long, stretchy strands. Gluten is what traps the carbon dioxide released by yeast in bread-making, allowing the dough to rise. The more you knead, the stronger and more elastic the gluten network becomes. This is why bread dough needs ten minutes of vigorous kneading to develop its full structure, while shortcrust pastry is handled as little as possible — you want a crumbly, short texture, not a tough, chewy one. Over-mixing pastry develops too much gluten and makes the final result tough.

Foam Formation

When egg whites are whisked vigorously, air is beaten into the liquid. The albumin proteins in the egg white are denatured by the mechanical action and form a thin, stable film around each air bubble. The result is a foam — a gas-in-liquid system where air is the gas and the egg white is the liquid. As you continue whisking, more and more air is incorporated until the foam reaches soft-peak stage, then stiff-peak stage. At stiff peak, the foam holds its shape. In a whisked sponge, the foam is folded into the batter; the trapped air expands in the oven, giving the cake its light texture. Over-whisking eventually breaks the protein film and the foam collapses — the egg white turns grainy and watery.

Key Fact

Four functional properties of proteins: denaturation (egg turns opaque in a hot pan); coagulation (quiche custard sets on baking); gluten formation (elastic dough develops when wheat flour is kneaded with water); foam formation (whisked egg whites trap air for a whisked sponge).

Functional Properties of Carbohydrates

Carbohydrates, especially starches and sugars, also have key functional properties that affect cooking outcomes. The spec identifies three: gelatinisation, dextrinisation and caramelisation. These three are frequently confused with each other in the exam — precise vocabulary is essential.

Gelatinisation

When starch granules are mixed with a cold liquid, they remain intact and separate. As the mixture is heated above about 60°C, the granules begin to absorb liquid and swell. Above 80°C they burst, releasing starch molecules that tangle together and thicken the liquid into a gel — this is gelatinisation. A roux-based béchamel sauce begins as butter and flour cooked together into a paste; when warm milk is added and the mixture is heated with constant stirring, the starch granules in the flour swell and burst, and the sauce thickens. The amount of starch added relative to the liquid controls the final viscosity: a thick pouring sauce uses less starch; a very stiff sauce or a setting agent uses more. This ratio is critical in sauce making.

Dextrinisation

Dextrinisation happens when starch on the surface of food is heated in dry conditions to above about 110°C. The starch breaks down into shorter molecules called dextrins, which are brown, have a toasted flavour and are partly soluble. The golden-brown crust on a loaf of bread is the result of dextrinisation: the starch in the outer layer of the dough is exposed to the dry heat of the oven and browns. Toast is an even clearer example — the pale bread surface goes from white to golden-brown to dark as the starch progressively dextrinises. This is not the same as the Maillard reaction, which involves both sugars and amino acids; dextrinisation involves starch only.

Caramelisation

Caramelisation occurs when sugars — not starch — are heated above approximately 160°C. The sugar molecules break down and recombine into hundreds of new compounds that produce shades of amber and brown, and a range of flavours from sweet and nutty to slightly bitter. Sprinkle sugar over a crème brûlée and apply a blowtorch: the sucrose melts and then caramelises into a hard, glass-like sheet. Roasted parsnips or carrots also caramelise where their natural sugars are exposed to the high, dry heat of an oven, which is why they develop a sweet, brown, almost sticky surface. Caramelisation requires higher temperatures than gelatinisation or dextrinisation and only involves sugars.

These three processes are routinely confused on the written paper. Here is the key to telling them apart:

Gelatinisation: starch + liquid + heat (60–80°C+) → granules swell and burst → mixture thickens. The ingredient is starch; the medium is water; the result is a gel or thick sauce.

Dextrinisation: starch + dry heat (110°C+) → starch breaks down to dextrins → brown colour and toasted flavour. The ingredient is starch; there is NO water; the result is surface browning (bread crust, toast).

Caramelisation: sugar + dry heat (160°C+) → sugar breaks down → brown colour and caramel flavour. The ingredient is sugar (not starch); there is NO water; the result is sweet, brown colour (crème brûlée top, roasted carrots).

Key Fact

Gelatinisation: starch granules absorb liquid and swell above 60°C, burst above 80°C, releasing starch molecules that tangle and thicken the liquid. Starch-to-liquid ratio controls viscosity — more starch gives a thicker result.

lesson_title: Fats, Fruit & Vegetables and Raising Agents
content_html:
Functional Properties of Fats and Oils

Fats and oils do far more than add flavour and calories to food. The spec identifies four functional properties: shortening, aeration, plasticity and emulsification. Each property explains why fat behaves differently in different recipes.

Shortening

When fat is rubbed into flour to make shortcrust pastry, the fat coats each flour particle. This coating prevents water from fully hydrating the flour proteins and stops gluten strands from linking together into a long, continuous network. The result is a “short” texture — crumbly, tender and melt-in-the-mouth rather than chewy and tough. The more fat is used relative to flour, the shorter (more crumbly) the pastry. This is why shortcrust pastry uses a 2:1 flour-to-fat ratio and why the fat must be rubbed in thoroughly and evenly before any water is added. If water is added before the fat has coated the flour particles, gluten begins to develop immediately and the pastry becomes tough.

Aeration

Solid fats such as butter and margarine can trap air when they are beaten with sugar — a process called creaming. During creaming, the sharp edges of sugar crystals cut tiny air pockets into the fat, which the fat holds firmly. When eggs and flour are folded into the creamed mixture and the cake is baked, these trapped air pockets expand and the cake rises. A properly creamed Victoria sponge mixture is pale, fluffy and almost doubled in volume — evidence that significant air has been incorporated. Aeration is temperature-sensitive: cold butter cannot trap air efficiently, and very warm butter releases the air before the cake sets. Butter at room temperature — around 18–20°C — is ideal for creaming.

Plasticity

Plasticity describes the ability of a fat to be shaped and spread at different temperatures. Unlike butter, which goes from rock-hard in the fridge to soft and spreadable at room temperature, a highly plastic fat remains workable across a range of temperatures. This property is important for laminated pastries such as croissants and puff pastry, where the fat needs to be cold enough to stay in solid layers rather than melt and blend into the dough, but pliable enough to be rolled and folded without cracking. A fat that lacks plasticity would either crumble and break through the dough layers when cold, or melt into the dough when warm, destroying the layers.

Emulsification

Oil and water do not naturally mix — they are immiscible. Shake them together and they separate immediately into two distinct layers. An emulsifier has a molecule with one end that attracts water and another end that attracts oil, allowing the two to blend into a stable, uniform mixture called an emulsion. The classic food example is mayonnaise: oil, egg yolk and lemon juice. The lecithin in egg yolk acts as a natural emulsifier, surrounding droplets of oil in a film that holds them suspended in the water-based lemon juice. In a simple French salad dressing (vinaigrette), no emulsifier is added; the dressing must be shaken immediately before use because it will separate on standing. Mustard, if added, contains small amounts of mucilage that act as a weak emulsifier and help the dressing stay blended for longer.

Key Fact

Four functional properties of fats and oils: shortening (pastry — fat coats flour, limits gluten); aeration (creamed cake — fat traps air with sugar); plasticity (croissant layers — fat works at a range of temperatures); emulsification (mayonnaise — egg yolk lecithin stabilises oil in water).

Enzymic Browning and Oxidation in Fruit and Vegetables

Fresh fruits and vegetables contain enzymes that cause specific chemical reactions when the plant cells are damaged. Understanding these reactions — and how to control them — is a key food-science skill.

Enzymic browning occurs when fruit or vegetables are cut, peeled or bruised. The physical damage breaks cell walls and releases enzymes — particularly polyphenol oxidases — that were previously separated from their substrates. These enzymes react with phenolic compounds in the cell, which then react with oxygen in the air to form brown-coloured melanin compounds. Cut apple, avocado, potato and artichoke all show this browning within minutes. The result is not dangerous, but it is visually unappealing and can signal that quality is declining.

The most effective way to prevent enzymic browning is to apply acid, typically lemon juice or vinegar. The acid lowers the pH around the enzyme, reducing its activity so the browning reaction slows significantly or stops. Brushing cut apple slices with lemon juice before adding them to a fruit salad is the standard practical solution. Submerging cut vegetables in cold water also limits enzymic browning by restricting access to oxygen. Blanching — briefly plunging vegetables into boiling water then cooling them rapidly in iced water — destroys the enzymes completely by denaturing them, which is why vegetables are blanched before freezing.

Oxidation is a related but distinct issue. When vitamin C (ascorbic acid) in vegetables is exposed to oxygen during preparation and cooking, it is chemically destroyed. Chopping vegetables increases the surface area exposed to air; boiling in water accelerates oxidation because heat and water together break down ascorbic acid rapidly. Minimising the time between preparation and cooking, and using water-conserving methods such as steaming or microwaving, helps reduce oxidative vitamin C loss.

Both involve oxygen, but they are different reactions. Enzymic browning is enzyme-driven: it requires the polyphenol oxidase enzyme released from damaged plant cells. You can stop enzymic browning by inactivating the enzyme (heat, acid, or lack of oxygen). Oxidation does not require an enzyme — it is a direct chemical reaction between vitamin C (or fats) and atmospheric oxygen. Storing cut vegetables in an airtight container slows oxidative vitamin C loss, but it will not prevent enzymic browning once the enzymes have been released. The distinction matters because the control methods differ: acid prevents enzymic browning but does not protect vitamin C from oxidative loss.

Raising Agents

Raising agents make baked goods light by introducing gas into the mixture before and during cooking. The gas expands when heated, creating a lighter, more open texture. There are four types of raising agent: chemical, mechanical, steam and biological.

Chemical Raising Agents

Chemical raising agents produce carbon dioxide gas through a chemical reaction. Baking powder is a mixture of bicarbonate of soda (an alkali) and cream of tartar (an acid); when moisture and heat are applied, they react together and release CO⊂2; bubbles. Bicarbonate of soda alone requires an acidic ingredient in the mixture (such as buttermilk, lemon juice or yoghurt) to activate it — without the acid, the baking soda can produce a soapy flavour and a yellowish tinge. Self-raising flour is plain flour with baking powder already incorporated at the manufacturing stage, making it a convenient single ingredient for home bakers. All three produce carbon dioxide that expands in the oven heat, causing the mixture to rise.

Mechanical Raising Agents

Mechanical raising agents physically incorporate air into the mixture. The air is the gas; the cooking method traps it in place. Techniques include whisking (egg whites for a meringue), creaming (butter and sugar for a Victoria sponge — see aeration above), folding (gently turning whisked egg whites into batter without losing air), sieving and rubbing in. In every case, the skill is incorporating maximum air without losing it through heavy-handed mixing.

Key Fact

Four raising agents: chemical (baking powder, bicarbonate of soda, self-raising flour — produce CO⊂2;); mechanical (whisking, creaming, folding, sieving, rubbing in — incorporate air); steam (water in the mixture turns to steam at 100°C — expands and raises); biological (yeast produces CO⊂2; by fermentation — raises bread).

Steam as a Raising Agent

Any moist mixture will produce steam when the water it contains reaches 100°C. This steam is a powerful raising agent. Choux pastry is the classic example: the mixture of butter, water, flour and eggs is piped into the oven; as the water in the mixture turns to steam, the pastry puffs and expands dramatically, creating a hollow shell. Yorkshire pudding batter works on exactly the same principle — the batter is poured into very hot fat and the water in the batter converts instantly to steam, causing the pudding to rise sharply. For steam to work effectively, the oven must be hot enough to convert the water to steam quickly, and the outer shell must be firm enough (through the coagulation of the egg protein) to hold its expanded shape.

Biological Raising Agents

Yeast is a living organism — a microorganism — that produces carbon dioxide gas through the process of fermentation. When yeast is mixed with warm water, flour and a small amount of sugar in bread dough, it feeds on the sugars and produces CO⊂2; as a by-product. The carbon dioxide is trapped by the gluten network in the dough, causing it to rise (prove). The dough is then knocked back (punched down to release some gas), shaped and proved again before baking. During baking, the high oven temperature kills the yeast and the CO⊂2; expands, giving the bread its final open, airy crumb. Yeast works much more slowly than chemical or steam raising agents — bread requires 1–2 hours of proving — but it also adds complex flavour compounds that chemical agents cannot replicate.

Each raising agent has a different speed, flavour impact and structural requirement:

Chemical: fast-acting once moisture and heat are applied; no flavour contribution (if balanced correctly); requires no protein structure before baking; used in cakes, scones, soda bread.

Mechanical: air is incorporated during mixing; no gas is produced by a chemical reaction; relies on the batter setting quickly enough in the oven to hold the air in place; requires careful folding technique.

Steam: only works in high-moisture mixtures; very powerful but requires very high oven temperature and a protein structure (coagulated egg) to hold the hollow shape; used in choux pastry, batter.

Biological: slowest — hours of fermentation required; adds complex flavour to bread; requires a gluten network to trap the CO⊂2;; killed by temperatures above about 60°C.

What Are Microorganisms?

Every time you leave a bowl of leftover chicken curry on the worktop overnight, you are giving microorganisms exactly what they need to multiply at speed. Microorganisms are invisible to the naked eye, but their effects — a furry grey patch on a bread loaf, a fizzing punnet of strawberries, the sour smell of yoghurt left too long — are very familiar. The three types you need to know are bacteria, yeasts and moulds. Each behaves differently and responds to conditions differently.

Bacteria are single-celled organisms that can divide roughly every 20 minutes under ideal conditions — meaning one bacterium can become millions in just a few hours. Yeasts are single-celled fungi that reproduce by budding and are responsible for fermentation (the process that makes bread rise and wine alcoholic). Moulds are multicellular fungi that grow as thread-like filaments called hyphae; you can see them on an over-ripe peach or a forgotten corner of bread.

What Microorganisms Need to Grow

Think of a microorganism’s needs as a simple checklist: food, moisture, warmth and time. Remove or limit any one factor and you slow or stop growth. This is the entire logic behind every food preservation and storage method you will study.

  • Food (nutrients): Bacteria and moulds thrive on protein and carbohydrates. High-protein moist foods — cooked chicken, shellfish, soft cheeses, cooked rice — are prime targets.
  • Moisture: Water availability (measured as water activity, aw) is critical. Dried foods like pasta, flour and biscuits have a very low aw, which is why they keep for months. Moist cooked foods have a high aw and spoil quickly.
  • Warmth: Most harmful bacteria multiply fastest between 5°C and 63°C — the temperature danger zone. Below 5°C growth slows dramatically; above 63°C most bacteria begin to die.
  • Time: Even in ideal conditions, it takes time for numbers to reach a dangerous level. A portion of cooked rice left at room temperature for two hours is much riskier than one left for twenty minutes.

Two additional factors affect growth: pH and oxygen. Most bacteria prefer a neutral pH (around 6.5–7.5). Very acidic foods like lemon juice or vinegar (low pH) slow bacterial growth — which is why pickling and marinating help preserve food. Some bacteria need oxygen (aerobic); others grow without it (anaerobic), which is why vacuum-packed meats can still carry a risk if temperature control fails.

Key Fact

Microorganisms need four things to multiply: food (nutrients), moisture, warmth (5°C–63°C danger zone) and time. Controlling any one of these slows or stops spoilage.

High-Risk Foods

High-risk foods are those that are ready to eat, moist and high in protein — meaning they support rapid bacterial growth and will not be cooked again before being eaten. The absence of that final heat treatment is what makes them dangerous: any bacteria already present will be consumed alive. Classic examples include cooked poultry, cooked rice, custards and cream-based desserts, soft cheeses, cooked shellfish and egg-based dishes such as quiche. A plate of leftover roast chicken that has been sitting at room temperature is a textbook high-risk food scenario.

Raw foods like uncooked chicken certainly carry bacteria (including campylobacter and salmonella), but cooking destroys those bacteria if the correct temperature is reached. The high-risk category refers specifically to foods that will be eaten without further cooking — so any bacteria present go straight into the body. A cooked chicken breast that has been left to cool slowly at room temperature is technically higher-risk than raw chicken that is about to go straight into the oven, because the cooked breast will be eaten as-is while bacteria multiply in the danger zone.

Enzymes and Food Spoilage

Enzymes are not microorganisms — they are biological catalysts produced by the cells of plants, animals and microorganisms themselves. In a freshly cut apple, enzymes called polyphenol oxidases react with oxygen in the air to produce brown pigments. This is enzymic browning, and it is why your apple slices turn brown within minutes of cutting. The same process causes bananas to go from yellow to brown and bruised pears to discolour.

Enzymic browning is not caused by bacteria or moulds — it is a purely chemical process. However, it is still spoilage because it affects the appearance, texture and sometimes the flavour of the food. You can control it by:

  • Acids: Squeezing lemon juice over cut fruit lowers the pH and deactivates the enzymes. This is why a fruit salad with a citrus dressing stays fresher-looking for longer.
  • Blanching: Briefly plunging vegetables into boiling water (blanching) denatures the enzymes by heat before freezing them. Without blanching, frozen peas or green beans would turn mushy and brown during storage because the enzymes would still be active even at –18°C.
  • Covering and minimising oxygen exposure: Wrapping cut fruit in cling film slows the reaction by limiting oxygen contact.
Key Fact

Enzymic browning is a chemical reaction controlled by enzymes — not by bacteria or moulds. Lemon juice (acid) and blanching (heat) are the two main controls. Vegetables must be blanched before freezing to prevent enzyme activity at –18°C.

Signs of Food Spoilage

Food spoils through three main routes: enzymic action, mould growth and yeast action. The signs are often obvious if you know what to look for.

  • Enzymic action: Ripening and softening of bananas (starch converts to sugars), browning of cut fruits and vegetables, softening of meat as proteases break down muscle fibres after slaughter.
  • Mould growth: Visible fuzzy patches (blue-green, white or black) on the surface of bread, soft cheeses, fruit and leftovers. Moulds produce thread-like hyphae and release spores; the visible fuzzy area is only the fruiting body — the hyphae may extend deeper into soft foods. Eating mouldy food is generally not recommended because some moulds produce toxic compounds called mycotoxins.
  • Yeast action: A fermenting, bubbling or fizzy quality, often with an alcoholic or sharp smell. This is why a punnet of squashed strawberries left in a warm kitchen develops a fizzing quality, or why opened fruit juice left for several days starts to ferment.

Not all microbial activity is harmful. Controlled use of microorganisms is at the heart of several traditional foods:

  • Moulds in blue cheese: Varieties such as Stilton and Roquefort get their characteristic blue-green veins from Penicillium mould cultures deliberately introduced into the cheese. The mould breaks down proteins and fats to create the distinctive strong, tangy flavour. The mould is controlled by specific temperature and moisture conditions during maturation.
  • Yeasts to raise bread: Baker’s yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) feeds on the sugars in bread dough and produces carbon dioxide gas and alcohol. The CO⊂2; is trapped by the gluten network in the dough, causing it to rise during proving. The alcohol evaporates during baking. Without yeast, bread would be dense and flat.
  • Bacteria in yoghurt and cheese: Lactic acid bacteria (such as Lactobacillus species) ferment the lactose in milk to produce lactic acid. This lowers the pH of the milk, causing the proteins to coagulate and thicken — producing yoghurt. The acidic environment also inhibits the growth of harmful bacteria, acting as a natural preservative. Hard cheeses use similar starter cultures alongside rennet to coagulate the milk proteins into curds.

Understanding that the same organisms that spoil food can also be harnessed to make it is an important distinction. The difference lies entirely in control: controlled conditions, starter cultures and careful monitoring of temperature, pH and moisture turn potential spoilage into valuable food products.

How Bacteria Get into Food

Bacterial contamination rarely arrives in one dramatic moment — it usually creeps in through a series of small mistakes. A chopping board used for raw chicken that is then used for salad leaves, a food handler who forgets to wash their hands after visiting the toilet, a pet walking across a kitchen surface — these are the real routes by which harmful bacteria reach the food we eat. Understanding the sources of bacterial contamination is the first step in preventing it.

The main sources of contamination are:

  • Other contaminated foods — particularly raw foods: Raw meat, poultry, eggs, seafood and unwashed vegetables all carry bacteria naturally. Raw chicken is one of the most significant sources of campylobacter in the UK. Even raw vegetables from the soil can carry bacteria such as e-coli if they have been in contact with animal manure during growing or harvesting.
  • Work surfaces and equipment: Bacteria survive on worktops, chopping boards, knives and mixing bowls for hours. A surface that was used for raw fish and wiped down with a damp cloth (rather than washed with hot soapy water) remains a contamination risk.
  • The people cooking: Hands are the main vector from person to food. Poor personal hygiene — sneezing over open food, touching the face, failing to wash hands after handling raw meat — is a leading cause of staphylococcus aureus contamination specifically.
  • Pests: Mice, rats, cockroaches and flies carry bacteria on their bodies and in their droppings. A fly landing on cooked food and then on raw meat transfers bacteria in both directions.
  • Waste food and rubbish: Decomposing food in bins creates a reservoir of bacteria that can spread if bins are stored near food preparation areas or if hands are not washed after handling waste.
Key Fact

The five sources of bacterial contamination are: other contaminated foods (especially raw meat, poultry, eggs, seafood and vegetables); work surfaces and equipment; the people cooking; pests; and waste food and rubbish.

The Five Food-Poisoning Bacteria

You need to know five specific bacteria by name — their typical sources, the conditions that favour them and the key control methods. A short-answer question asking you to name two and give their sources is very common. Memorise all five: campylobacter, e-coli, salmonella, listeria and staphylococcus aureus. Students who know only salmonella consistently lose marks on this topic.

Campylobacter is found primarily in raw and undercooked poultry, particularly chicken. It is also found in unpasteurised milk, contaminated water and the intestines of farm animals. It is responsible for the majority of bacterial food poisoning cases in the UK each year. The key control is thorough cooking — campylobacter is destroyed when poultry reaches an internal temperature of 75°C throughout. Do not wash raw chicken: washing spreads campylobacter-laden droplets up to a metre around the sink. Campylobacter does not multiply particularly fast in food at room temperature; its main risk is survival from undercooking.

E-coli (Escherichia coli): Most strains of e-coli are harmless gut bacteria, but certain strains (particularly E. coli O157) produce toxins that cause severe illness. Sources include undercooked ground beef (minced meat), contaminated water, and raw vegetables grown in soil fertilised with animal manure. Control methods: thorough cooking of minced meat to 75°C throughout; washing raw vegetables; good hand hygiene; pasteurising milk.

Salmonella: Found in raw poultry, raw eggs, raw meat and some unpasteurised dairy products. Contamination can come from the inside of an egg if the laying hen was infected, which is why runny fried eggs carry a risk if the eggs are not from a Lion Code flock. Control: thorough cooking to 75°C; good personal hygiene when handling raw eggs; refrigerating raw poultry separately from cooked foods.

Listeria (Listeria monocytogenes) is unusual because it can multiply at refrigerator temperatures — between 0°C and 5°C — making it a particular threat in chilled ready-to-eat foods. Sources include soft mould-ripened cheeses (such as Brie and Camembert), pâté, cold deli meats and smoked fish. Listeria is especially dangerous for pregnant women, where it can cause miscarriage or serious illness in the newborn. Control: keep chilled food below 5°C and consume within use-by date; vulnerable groups should avoid high-risk products.

Staphylococcus aureus is carried naturally on human skin, in the nose, throat and hair. It reaches food when food handlers sneeze, cough, touch their face or have skin infections such as cuts or boils. Once in the food, it multiplies and produces toxins that are heat-resistant — meaning cooking the food again will not destroy the toxin even if the bacteria are killed. High-risk situations include cooked rice, egg mayonnaise, and cream-filled pastries left at room temperature. Control: strict personal hygiene; keeping food below 5°C or above 63°C; covering cuts with blue waterproof plasters.

Key Fact

The five food-poisoning bacteria you must know: campylobacter (raw poultry), e-coli (undercooked minced beef, contaminated water), salmonella (raw poultry, raw eggs), listeria (soft cheeses, chilled ready-to-eat meats — can grow at fridge temperature), staphylococcus aureus (human skin/nose/throat, cooked foods at room temperature).

Symptoms of Food Poisoning

Food poisoning is caused either by the bacteria themselves infecting the gut, or by toxins they have already produced in the food before it is eaten. The general symptoms are consistent across most types, although their severity and timing vary:

  • Nausea (feeling sick)
  • Vomiting
  • Diarrhoea
  • Stomach cramps and abdominal pain
  • Fever (raised body temperature)
  • Headache and general malaise

Symptoms typically develop between one hour and several days after eating contaminated food, depending on the bacterium. Staphylococcus aureus toxin can cause symptoms within one to six hours because the toxin is already present in the food. Campylobacter infections typically take two to five days to develop because the bacteria must first establish in the gut. Most healthy adults recover within a few days, but young children, elderly people, pregnant women and those with weakened immune systems can develop serious complications, including dehydration and, in rare cases, kidney failure.

lesson_title: Principles of Food Safety — Buying, Storing and Preparing
content_html:
Temperature: The Most Important Food Safety Control

If you could only remember one food safety principle, it would be this: temperature controls bacterial growth. The Food Standards Agency (FSA) publishes specific temperature guidelines that underpin every aspect of safe food handling, and the written paper tests exact figures. Vague answers like “keep it cold” or “cook it until hot” will not earn marks. Memorise these numbers.

Key Fact

FSA temperature guidelines: Freezing: –18°C — bacteria cannot multiply. Chilling: 0 to below 5°C — bacterial growth is very slow. Danger zone: 5 to 63°C — bacteria multiply rapidly. Cooking and reheating: 75°C — most harmful bacteria are destroyed.

The temperature danger zone is the range 5°C to 63°C. This is why food should never be left at room temperature (typically 18–22°C, well inside the danger zone) for longer than necessary. Bacteria can double in number every 20 minutes at room temperature — a portion of cooked rice left on a worktop for two hours can contain many millions more bacteria than one put straight into the fridge.

Buying and Storing Food Safely

Safe food handling begins at the point of purchase, not when you get home. When shopping, always:

  • Check date marks before buying. ‘Use by’ dates apply to high-risk foods such as raw meat, cooked meat products and soft cheeses — consuming after this date could harm health. ‘Best before’ dates apply to lower-risk foods such as tinned goods, dried pasta and frozen peas; the food remains safe after this date but may decline in quality.
  • Pack raw meat and fish in separate bags from ready-to-eat foods to prevent drip contamination.
  • Choose chilled and frozen foods last in a supermarket shop and transport them in insulated bags to minimise the time spent in the danger zone.

‘Use by’ is a food safety date. Eating food after its use-by date is a genuine health risk, regardless of whether it looks or smells fine — harmful bacteria do not always cause visible or olfactory changes. ‘Best before’ is a quality date. After a ‘best before’ date, the food may be less flavoursome, have a different texture or lose some nutritional value, but it is not automatically unsafe. A can of tomatoes three days past its best-before date is still safe to eat; a pack of cooked prawns one day past its use-by date should be discarded. In an exam, be precise: low-risk ambient foods carry ‘best before’ labels; high-risk perishable foods carry ‘use by’ labels.

At home, correct use of domestic refrigerators and freezers is essential:
